reason: The examples describe the individual flowers or the male part, not the spike. A rule would need to tell whether the statement is about the whole inflorescence or about its flowers.
A minute or small pappus is normal, and the examples fit.
A leaf blade or base can flare, and the examples fit.
Succulent roots and taproots are common.
Whether an extrafloral nectary is present or absent is a normal trait. The examples mostly say 'absent', which is the opposite value, so the absent value needs its own pair.
The examples are about concave sides, which is a normal shape quality. The part has no label in the lexicon, so I could not check it against the part itself.
The depth in the examples belongs to the umbilicus (the fruit's basal pit), not to the whole fruit. The pair exists only through a wrong reading of the part.

'Hyaline' wings belong to the rachilla, which is not clearly a higher order axis. Hyaline also means thin and translucent. A rule would need to say which part carries the wings and whether hyaline maps to transparent.
'Persistent' bracts are non-deciduous, which matches.
Cells can be narrow, and the examples fit.
'Stout' means thick and sturdy, and it applies to different parts. The part has no label, and all the statements come from a single flora. A rule would need to know the part.
Ellipsoid cones are roughly prolate. Strictly, prolate means elongated with a round cross-section, so this is a loose match.
Protogyny is a trait of the flower.
Lobes can be subtriangular.
'Rigid' means inflexible. One example is about the hairs of the involucre rather than the involucre itself, but the pair is meaningful.
Roots and taproots can be narrow.
'Irregular' can mean an irregular branching pattern or an irregular stem shape, and those are different qualities. A rule would need to separate the two readings.
Filiform lobes are a normal shape.
A chartaceous (papery) palea is normal.
A rough or scabrous margin is normal. Some examples ('coarse teeth') are really about teeth, not texture.
'Angled' (ridged) is not 'bent'. The PATO term means something else, so the pair comes from a wrong reading.
Flower colour is normal. One example is about the tepals, but they are part of the flower.
A sessile lip or base is normal.
Auricles can be narrow.
Elliptic pinnae are normal.
Stipules can be winged or flanged. Some examples are about margins, but the quality fits.
A lobe apex or margin can be convex.
A reflexed mid-lobe is normal.
The examples are cell widths given as measurements.
'Pale' is close to low saturation. The match is loose, but the pair is meaningful for peristome teeth.
'1–4 per perichaetium' is a count of setae per perichaetium, not an amount of the part. A rule for counted parts (config/flora_counted_parts.tsv) should handle it, and a term should not.
Ciliate bracts are normal.
Hairy pinnae or rachis parts are normal.
The examples are about leaf veins ('veins weak'), not vascular bundles. The part is wrong, and the veins should map to a vein class.
Oblanceolate lobes are normal.
A keeled calyx is normal.
Cordate lobes or lobe bases are normal.
The examples are about branches and rays of the inflorescence, not the ray flower. A rule would need to tell ray flowers from inflorescence rays.
A wide or broadened calyx is normal.
'Entire' describes a margin, not a stem. The examples are about margins, so this is a wrong part.
Coriaceous (leathery) is a normal texture for leaves and similar parts.
The examples are pulvinus lengths given as measurements.
A length-to-width ratio of a leaflet is normal.
An inconspicuous pedicel is normal.
Deciduous stigmas are normal.
Keels on a part are normal.
Dark nodes are normal.
A glabrous shoot is normal. Some examples ('Lower sepal and spur') look misattributed, though.
A thread-like (filamentous) pedicel is normal.
The stylopodium can have a colour.
'Depressed' means sunken, not curved. Arcuate veins do have curvature. A rule would need to tell sunken from curved.
A lanate or woolly leaf surface is normal.
Shape is a valid attribute for this part. The examples list specific shapes, so a specific value is better when one exists.
'Characteristic' is the root quality term and says nothing. The examples (entire or erose, ciliate) are specific states and need their own terms.
A lemma can be longer than the glumes.
A hairy base or throat is normal.
An oblate inflorescence or infructescence is meaningful.
The examples (fusiform-conic, ovoid) are specific solid shapes. 'Convex 3-D shape' is too generic. A rule would need to map them to specific shapes.
Leaflets or the rachis between them can be winged.
A small rhizome is normal.
